title: The Ark Comes to Jerusalem
overview: David brings the ark, the sacred chest that stood for God's presence, to his new capital, through a sudden death, a long pause, a joyful second attempt, and a bitter clash with his wife Michal.

parts.label: A grand procession begins (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: The ark, a sacred chest described as the place where the LORD sits enthroned, had stayed for years in a private house after the Philistines returned it, and David now sets out to bring it to Jerusalem with music and a huge crowd. They load it on a new oxcart, though Israel's law said Levites, the tribe set apart for worship duties, were to carry it on their shoulders.

parts.label: Uzzah is struck down (vv. 6-8)
parts.note: When the oxen stumble, Uzzah grabs the ark to steady it and God strikes him dead; the rare Hebrew word for his act is translated as "irreverence" or "error," and the text gives no fuller reason. Interpreters often point to an earlier law that even the Levites who carried the holy things must not touch them, but many readers still find this hard, and David himself reacts with anger, naming the place "Perez Uzzah," meaning "outbreak against Uzzah."

parts.label: The ark waits three months (vv. 9-11)
parts.note: Now afraid, David leaves the ark at the house of Obed-Edom "the Gittite" rather than take it home; the title can mean someone from the Philistine city of Gath, though some think it points to Gath-rimmon, a town given to the Levites. Instead of disaster, that household is blessed.

parts.label: A second attempt (vv. 12-16)
parts.note: This time people carry the ark, and after its first six steps David offers a bull and a fattened calf as sacrifices. He dances with all his strength in a linen ephod, a simple garment linked with priests, while his wife Michal, King Saul's daughter, watches from a window with contempt.

parts.label: The ark settles in a tent (vv. 17-19)
parts.note: The ark is placed in a tent David set up, and he offers sacrifices, including fellowship offerings that were partly eaten as a shared celebration meal. He blesses the crowd and gives every man and woman bread, a raisin cake, and a third item the translations render differently, as a cake of dates or a portion of meat, because the Hebrew word is uncertain.

parts.label: Michal and David clash (vv. 20-23)
parts.note: Michal mocks David for uncovering himself before servant girls like a common show off, and he replies that he danced before the LORD, who chose him over her father, and he will gladly look even less dignified. The closing line that she never had children is not explained, and readers differ on whether it means punishment, a broken marriage, or simply the end of Saul's line through her.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to understand Uzzah's death: some see it as a just and necessary lesson about God's holiness, while others see it as a troubling story that reflects how ancient Israel understood holiness and needs to be read alongside the rest of the Bible.
think: Is it possible to care about something so much that you stop caring how you look to others, and is that a good or a bad thing?
